title: The Plank-Carrier's Song (with Commentary)
excerpt: (Recorded from Master Hanshan's Collection of Dream Wanderings) Annotated by Zhanran

inline.s: (Recorded from Master Hanshan's Collection of Dream Wanderings)
Annotated by Zhanran

Chan practice passes through three stages: dwelling solely on the huatou (all thoughts converge into one), the state where not a single thought arises (the one returns to nothing), and seeing the mind and realizing one's true nature (directly realizing the original nature).
Of these three stages, Master Hanshan taught:

“When you settle firmly upon the huatou, all idle thoughts and distracting notions are cut off at once, like severing a tangled thread; they are never allowed to arise again, and wherever they rise they instantly dissolve.
Only a single thought remains, clear and solitary in its brightness,
like the noon sun in the sky; deluded thoughts no longer arise, dull confusion retreats of itself, and there is stillness within awareness.
When you look
to the point where not a single thought arises, past and future are cut off, and the present stands alone in solitude
suddenly the pitch barrel is shattered and you see your original face at once

. Then body and mind and the whole world sink into stillness in that very moment, like flowers of emptiness whose shadows fall away; the ten directions are perfectly luminous, forming one great treasury of radiant light. Only this is the time of arriving home; in daily life it is present before you, bright and round and clear, leaving nothing more to doubt. Only then do you believe that your own mind has always been thus — no different from the ground that all Buddhas and patriarchs of old personally enjoy.”
(From the Collection of Dream Wanderings,
“Essentials of Buddha-Recitation and Chan Investigation”)
In this teaching, “Only a single thought remains,
(only the one thought of the huatou),

clear and solitary in its brightness” describes all thoughts converging into one; “when you look to the point where not a single thought arises, past and future are cut off and the present stands alone” describes the one returning to nothing
(even that single thought of the huatou is gone);

“suddenly the pitch barrel is shattered and you see your original face at once” describes seeing the mind and realizing one's true nature. “Body and mind and the whole world sink into stillness in that very moment, like flowers of emptiness whose shadows fall away; the ten directions are perfectly luminous, forming one great treasury of radiant light” is a depiction of the state of seeing the mind and realizing one's true nature. “Only this is the time of arriving home” explains that the goal of Chan investigation is seeing the mind and realizing one's true nature
(directly realizing the original nature)
And after seeing the mind and realizing one's true nature, one must undertake the work of preserving and sustaining it.

the plank-carrier” (danbanhan) is a term used in the Chan school. Originally it referred to a laborer who carries a wooden plank on his back; because he can see only what lies ahead and not to either side, the Chan school uses it as a metaphor for someone whose view is one-sided and cannot embrace the whole. Here it refers to those who, in Chan practice, rest content with a small attainment: having achieved “the one returning to nothing” (not a single thought arising), they take it for the ultimate — like someone carrying a plank on his back, seeing only one side and not the whole, mistaking the conjured city for the place of treasures. Hence the song says:
“Alas, they sit upon the pure white ground
(lingering in the state where not a single thought arises)
, unwilling to let go, taking it for something extraordinary, not knowing that it has instead become an obstruction to the Dharma.” “I urge you, do not carry it
(do not cling to the state of “the one returning to nothing”)

[The conjured city] A city conjured by illusion. It comes from the parable of the conjured city in the Lotus Sutra. The parable of the conjured city says: the place where all sentient beings attain Buddhahood is the place of treasures, but the road to it is steep, dangerous, and long. Fearing that travelers would grow weary and turn back, the Buddha conjured a city midway so that they might rest for a while, gather their strength, and then press straight on to the place of treasures. The Buddha wished all sentient beings to realize the fruit of Buddhahood, yet because their hearts are timid and their strength weak, unable to bear the burden, he first taught the nirvāṇa of the lesser vehicle, so that by attaining this nirvāṇa they might rest for a while; from there they rouse the greater resolve and advance toward the true place of treasures, the nirvāṇa of the Great Vehicle (the fruit of Buddhahood).
The Dharma grotto of Mount Jing

(the Jizhao Hermitage on Mount Jing was Master Daguan's monastery; Master Hanshan came there to mourn Master Daguan and to perform the cremation rites for him. During this time, to all who came seeking instruction he gave Dharma talks, and he composed the “Plank-Carrier's Song”)
, where since the great master Dahui
revived the way of the Linji school
(in the Song dynasty Chan Master Dahui Zonggao revived the Linji school here)

, the life of wisdom has been continued and each generation has not lacked worthy heirs. Of late the Chan school has grown desolate, and its echoes have long fallen silent. Recently, however, a host of practitioners of investigation filled the mountain, and some reached the point where a single thought breaks through to the ground
, with the essence manifesting directly before them and attaining great freedom. Alas, they sit upon the pure white ground
(lingering in the state where not a single thought arises)

, unwilling to let go, taking it for something extraordinary, not knowing that it has instead become an obstruction to the Dharma — what the teachings call the hindrance of what is known. Hence an ancient worthy said: “Even if you reach the point of
(even if you attain)

‘the bright moon in a cold pool, the bell's sound in the still night, undiminished by striking, undisturbed by ripples,’ it is still an affair on this shore of birth and death.” As it is said, it is easy to set foot in the thorny thicket
(it is easy to attain all thoughts converging into one, and the one returning to nothing)
, but hard to turn the body beneath the moonlit curtain
(it is hard to go beyond the one returning to nothing and directly realize the original nature)
. This is called ‘clinging to the top of the pole’
(one who does not turn beneath the moonlit curtain is called one who ‘clings to the top of the hundred-foot pole’)

. Even in the still depths of stagnant water one is not permitted to sit and dwell — how much less those who, before reaching the breakthrough, chance upon the lightning-flash samādhi and take it for attainment, toying with the shadow of the discriminating consciousness! This resting content with a small gain in Chan practice is the common ailment of ancient and modern times. Fearing that these views would fall into the vulgar stream of worldly truth and spread
(fearing that these worldly views of resting content with little would spread widely)
, deceiving and misleading many, whenever anyone came seeking instruction I smilingly composed the ‘Plank-Carrier's Song’ to show them.
[The lightning-flash samādhi] Describes an extremely brief samādhi, vanishing in an instant like a flash of lightning. [Clinging to the top of the pole] Chan Master Daoyuan wrote in a verse:
“The man who does not move atop the hundred-foot pole
(one who has attained the one returning to nothing)
, though he has gained entry, it is not yet true; atop the hundred-foot pole he must take one step further
(directly realizing the original nature)
, and the worlds of the ten directions become his whole body.”

(Record of the Transmission of the Lamp Compiled in the Jingde Era) [The unmoving man] “Unmoving” means the thoughts do not move (no thought arises), that is, not a single thought arises. “The unmoving man” is one in whom not a single thought arises.
Chan Master Dahui said:

“Nowadays people mostly attain a state where body and mind are quiescent, where past and future are cut off, where they rest and desist, where one thought endures for ten thousand years, like the incense burner in an old temple, cold and silent — and they take this for the ultimate. Little do they know that they are being veiled by this sublime state, so that their own right knowledge and vision cannot manifest, and their spiritual powers and radiance cannot unfold.”
(Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dahui Pujue)

[One thought enduring ten thousand years] “One thought enduring ten thousand years” here describes the state where all thoughts converge into one; “to desist” (qu) means to extinguish. “One thought enduring ten thousand years, then desist” means to extinguish even that single thought within the state of all thoughts converging into one, and so enter the state of no-thought. [The incense burner of an old temple] The incense burner of an old temple (the little remaining incense fire in an old temple) is a metaphor for a mind that is pure and undivided — this is the state of all thoughts converging into one. “The incense burner of an old temple, then desist” (removing even that little remaining incense fire in the old temple) is a metaphor for the one returning to nothing, entering the state of no-thought. [A single strip of white silk] White silk (bailian): white satin. Here white silk is likewise a metaphor for a mind pure and undivided — the state of all thoughts converging into one. “A single strip of white silk, then desist” means to remove even the single remaining thought (the one returning to nothing), and so enter the state of no-thought.
The Venerable Xuyun taught:
“There are those who,
(some people),

having reached this state, with some slight mastery over their practice and without encountering any impenetrable realm, suppose that their ignorance is fully severed and their practice has arrived home; little do they know that they pass their days sitting within the cave of ignorance without being aware of it. Suddenly encountering some realm, they cannot break through it and cannot be their own masters, and as before they are carried away by it — is that not a pity! Or there are those who, having reached the state where genuine doubt appears before them and a little wisdom arises in the void, having grasped a few ancient cases, put down their doubt and suppose themselves to be greatly enlightened, chanting poems and verses, glancing and raising their brows, calling themselves good teachers. Such people deceive themselves and deceive others, and their transgression is boundless. Again, there are those who misunderstand the meaning of Bodhidharma's ‘Externally put to rest all conditions; inwardly let the mind be without panting; with a mind like a wall, one may enter the Way,’ and the Sixth Patriarch's ‘Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, at just this moment, what is the original face of the Venerable Ming?’, and so take sitting at the edge of a withered tree as the final principle. Such people take the conjured city for the place of treasures, and mistake a foreign land for their native home.”
(See
The Chan Dharma of Xuyun
Master Hanshan taught:
“If in this matter
(the single path upward)

you do not lay down body and mind and investigate with bitter intensity until the waters run dry and the mountains come to an end, you will never reach a conclusion. Even when you do reach the place where waters run dry and mountains end, the ancients called it the still depths of stagnant water, and also the lair of the mysterious and wonderful. If you do not turn your head and shift your mind, what lies before you is like an iron wall or a silver mountain — this is a time of gaining strength, not a place of genuine enjoyment. The ancients' use of mind was not to die all the way to the end; one must stir to life from within death, and the key lies in turning the mechanism and shifting the position. Hence it is said: The man who sits atop the hundred-foot pole, though he has gained entry, it is not yet true; atop the hundred-foot pole he must take yet another step, and the great chiliocosm will manifest his whole body.”
(From the Collection of Dream Wanderings,
“Instructions to Chan Practitioner Zhuanyu Heng”; for commentary, see
Record of Master Hanshan's Teachings
[The single path upward] The utmost point of the Chan school (transcending sage and ordinary, leaving birth and death) is called the single path upward.
The song goes:
Plank-carrier, O plank-carrier, why let it so bitterly deceive you?
(How could you be deceived by this state where not a single thought arises, taking it for the ultimate?)
You seek only a light load on your shoulder
(caring only for the ease and self-contentment of this state where not a single thought arises),
never mind the stumbling of your heels
(not knowing that afflictions are unsevered and birth and death unfinished)
Even if
(even if you)
you carry it to the point before birth
(seeing your nature),
half of you is already hidden away by it
(seeing only the conjured city and not the place of treasures)
This plank, a cangue about your neck — all your bones and flesh belong to it.
If you do not cast it off quickly and soon, it will be a true enemy for a hundred thousand myriads of kalpas
(it will mislead you through a hundred thousand myriads of kalpas of transmigration through birth and death)
Sitting, it burdens you; walking, it burdens you
(sitting you are weighed down by it, walking you are weighed down by it),
a clear obstruction — why do you not awaken to it
(clearly this is an obstruction, why do you not yet awaken to it)
Only because at the start you mistook the false for the true
(taking the conjured city for the place of treasures),
demons and phantoms breed in the clear gate and the quiet house.
Open your eyes, you see it; close your eyes, you see it — in broad daylight, lightning flashes across the void.
[Lightning flashing across the void in broad daylight] This says that the state of the one returning to nothing is not true unbornness.
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:

“Not seeing a single dharma, yet keeping the view of nothingness, is much like drifting clouds hiding the sun's face; not knowing a single dharma, yet guarding the knowledge of emptiness, is just like lightning flashing across the void.”
(See
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch: A Detailed Commentary
The gandharva city
(a phantom city, like a mirage)
appears as a shadow in the void, and the foolish child takes it for a palace of the gods.
If you would be light, you must let go — what price would a stinking dead toad fetch?
Bring black beans to trade for eyes; from fish eyes you must discern the true from the false.
There is a road, the best to travel, broad and level as a balance scale
(like the great highway in times of peace, with no bandits and easy to walk)
Only do not linger by the flowers and willows on the wayside, and you are sure, in years to come, to enter the imperial capital
(the place of treasures)
Give up body and life like the great earth; from oxen, horses, camels, and donkeys you need not turn aside.
If you can in one throw pass beyond Mount Sumeru, then forests of swords and mountains of knives are but child's play.
If you cherish it
(if you cling to this state of the one returning to nothing),
it will harm you; its encumbrance comes largely from the effort of tending it.
One day you shatter the crystal vase, and the great earth and its mountains and rivers are all crushed to dust
(directly realizing the original nature)
I urge you, carry it not — the skull that has sweat dries again in that very moment.
Manifesting bodies and scattering forms by the hundreds of thousands of myriads, from now on you will never again enter the gate of death.
